body:
What is atmospheric pressure?

The atmosphere consists of gases that have mass and are held around the Earth by gravity. These gases exert pressure on the Earth's surface and on objects within the atmosphere.

Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted per unit area by the weight of the column of air above a given surface.

Atmospheric pressure is measured using a barometer. Meteorologists commonly express it in hectopascals (hPa) or millibars (mb). Both units have the same numerical value.

  • Standard atmospheric pressure at mean sea level: approximately 1013.25 hPa or 1013.25 mb.
  • Equivalent mercury column: 760 mm or 76 cm.
  • 1 hPa = 1 mb.

Actual atmospheric pressure at sea level varies according to atmospheric conditions. The standard value is a reference value rather than a constant pressure observed everywhere.

Factors influencing atmospheric pressure

Temperature

When air is heated, it expands and becomes less dense. In the open atmosphere, this warmer air tends to rise, and the resulting redistribution of air may reduce surface pressure. Conversely, cooling makes air denser and encourages sinking, which can contribute to higher surface pressure.

This relationship helps explain the development of low pressure near the warm equatorial region and high pressure near the cold poles.

Altitude

Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing altitude because the weight of the overlying column of air decreases. Consequently, mountain regions generally experience lower atmospheric pressure than places near sea level.

Humidity

Water vapour has a lower molecular mass than the principal gases of dry air. At the same temperature and pressure, moist air is therefore less dense than dry air. However, humidity alone does not determine surface atmospheric pressure.

Atmospheric circulation

Large-scale upward and downward movements of air redistribute atmospheric mass. As a result, pressure differences can develop even when they cannot be explained by local surface temperature alone.

How pressure differences produce winds

The Earth receives unequal amounts of solar energy at different latitudes. Equatorial regions generally receive more solar energy per unit area than polar regions. This unequal heating contributes to differences in temperature and atmospheric pressure.

Differences in pressure produce a pressure gradient force, which accelerates air from regions of higher pressure towards regions of lower pressure. The horizontal movement of air is called wind.

The pressure gradient is the change in atmospheric pressure over a given horizontal distance. Other conditions being similar, a stronger pressure gradient produces stronger winds.

Isobars are lines joining places having equal atmospheric pressure on a weather map. Closely spaced isobars indicate a strong pressure gradient, whereas widely spaced isobars indicate a weak pressure gradient.

Convergence, divergence and weather

When surface winds move towards a common region, the movement is called convergence. When they spread outward from a region, the movement is called divergence.

Surface low-pressure regions are generally associated with convergence and ascending air. As moist air rises, it expands and cools. Water vapour may condense, producing clouds and precipitation. The tall thunderclouds frequently observed over warm equatorial oceans illustrate this process.

Surface high-pressure regions are generally associated with descending air and divergence. Descending air becomes warmer through compression, reducing its relative humidity and discouraging cloud formation.

These are general associations rather than absolute rules. Rainfall also requires sufficient moisture and suitable atmospheric conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
  • Standard sea-level pressure is approximately 1013.25 hPa.
  • Pressure gradient force acts from higher pressure towards lower pressure.
  • Closely spaced isobars indicate a stronger pressure gradient.
  • Surface convergence generally favours ascent; surface divergence generally accompanies subsidence.
  • Trap: All high-pressure regions are not cold, and all low-pressure regions are not hot.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 4: Air, pp. 24–26; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9: Atmospheric Circulation and Weather Systems, pp. 76–79; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 10: Winds, pp. 67–70. Online textbook copies consulted on 28 November 2026 where project-library text was unreadable.]

title: Atmospheric Pressure and the Origin of Winds

body:
Meaning and distribution of pressure belts

Atmospheric pressure varies across the Earth's surface. On a global scale, regions of relatively high and low pressure form broad zones extending approximately along latitudes. These zones are known as planetary pressure belts.

The idealised global distribution contains 7 major pressure belts: 1 equatorial low-pressure belt, 2 subtropical high-pressure belts, 2 subpolar low-pressure belts and 2 polar high-pressure belts.

Thus, the Earth has 4 high-pressure belts and 3 low-pressure belts in the conventional model.

Formation and characteristics of the pressure belts

1. Equatorial low-pressure belt

This belt occurs near the Equator, approximately around 0° latitude. Intense solar heating causes warm, moisture-bearing air to rise. Surface winds converge towards this region, maintaining the ascending circulation.

As the rising air cools, condensation and convectional rainfall frequently occur. The belt is therefore associated with humid conditions, extensive cloud formation and frequent thunderstorms.

The equatorial low is primarily thermally induced, meaning that strong heating is a major cause of its formation.

The region is traditionally known as the doldrums because its surface winds are often weak or variable.

2. Subtropical high-pressure belts

These occur near 30° N and 30° S. They are also called tropical high-pressure belts in some geographical classifications.

Air that rises near the Equator moves towards higher latitudes in the upper troposphere. Part of this air descends in the subtropics, establishing relatively high surface pressure.

These highs are primarily dynamically induced, meaning that they develop mainly through large-scale atmospheric circulation rather than simply through local surface cooling.

Descending air becomes warmer through compression, making condensation and rainfall less likely. This helps explain why several major deserts, including the Sahara and Arabian deserts, occur in the subtropical latitudes.

The subtropical high-pressure regions near 30° N and 30° S are traditionally called the horse latitudes.

3. Subpolar low-pressure belts

These occur near 60° N and 60° S. Relatively warm westerly winds from the middle latitudes encounter cold easterly winds originating in polar regions.

The boundary between these contrasting air masses is known as the polar front. Atmospheric convergence and ascent in this region help maintain relatively low surface pressure.

The subpolar lows are mainly dynamically induced. They are associated with frequent atmospheric disturbances and unsettled weather.

Their existence demonstrates that low pressure does not necessarily require high surface temperatures.

4. Polar high-pressure belts

These occur near 90° N and 90° S, around the geographical poles. Weak solar heating and extremely low temperatures favour the development of cold, dense air that tends to descend.

The polar highs are primarily thermally induced through intense cooling. Air flows outward from these high-pressure regions towards the subpolar lows.

Polar regions generally receive little precipitation because their air contains relatively little water vapour and descending motion discourages cloud formation.

Thermal and dynamic pressure belts

Pressure beltPrincipal originAir movement
Equatorial lowThermal: heatingAscending
Subtropical highDynamic: circulationDescending
Subpolar lowDynamic: circulationAscending
Polar highThermal: coolingDescending

Approximate latitudinal extent

The conventional positions of 0°, 30°, 60° and 90° are useful reference latitudes, not rigid boundaries.

A more detailed school-level classification expresses the approximate extent of the belts as follows:

  • Equatorial low-pressure belt: 5° N to 5° S.
  • Subtropical high-pressure belts: 20° to 30° in both hemispheres.
  • Subpolar low-pressure belts: 60° to 70° in both hemispheres.
  • Polar high-pressure belts: 80° to 90° in both hemispheres.

Actual positions and widths vary with season, the distribution of continents and oceans, and atmospheric circulation. On real weather maps, these belts may appear as separate high-pressure and low-pressure centres rather than continuous bands.

Prelims focus

  • 7 pressure belts: 4 high-pressure and 3 low-pressure belts.
  • Equatorial low near 0°; subtropical highs near 30° N and S.
  • Subpolar lows near 60° N and S; polar highs near 90° N and S.
  • Equatorial low and polar highs are primarily thermal in origin.
  • Subtropical highs and subpolar lows are primarily dynamic in origin.
  • Trap: Pressure belts are not permanently fixed at their idealised latitudes.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 4: Air, Fig. 4.4, p. 25; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9, pp. 77–80; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 10: Winds, pp. 68–70; UK Met Office, Global Circulation Patterns. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]

title: The Seven Major Pressure Belts of the Earth

body:
Why winds do not follow a straight north–south path

Pressure differences cause air to move towards lower pressure. However, the Earth rotates from west to east. When atmospheric motion is observed relative to this rotating Earth, the moving air appears to be deflected from its original direction.

The Coriolis effect is the apparent deflection of moving objects, including winds and ocean currents, resulting from the rotation of the Earth.

The associated apparent force is known as the Coriolis force, named after the French mathematician and physicist Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis.

Direction of deflection

For large-scale horizontal atmospheric movement, the direction of Coriolis deflection follows a consistent hemispheric rule:

  • Northern Hemisphere: deflection towards the right of the direction of motion.
  • Southern Hemisphere: deflection towards the left of the direction of motion.

This hemispheric rule is also known in geography as Ferrel's law.

Right and left must always be understood relative to the direction in which the air is travelling. They do not represent fixed geographical directions.

For example, a northward-moving wind in the Northern Hemisphere is deflected towards the east, whereas a southward-moving wind in the same hemisphere is deflected towards the west.

Variation of the Coriolis effect

Effect of latitude

For horizontal motion at the same speed, the magnitude of the Coriolis effect increases with distance from the Equator towards either pole.

  • At 0° latitude: the horizontal Coriolis effect is zero.
  • At intermediate latitudes: its magnitude increases towards the poles.
  • At 90° N and 90° S: its magnitude is maximum for a given horizontal speed.

The Coriolis effect changes direction when moving from one hemisphere into the other.

Effect of wind speed

At the same latitude, a faster-moving air mass experiences a greater Coriolis force than a slower-moving air mass.

The Coriolis effect acts on air that is already moving. It does not itself initiate wind movement. The pressure gradient force normally provides the initial acceleration.

Forces controlling near-surface winds

ForcePrincipal effect
Pressure gradient forceAccelerates air towards lower pressure
Coriolis forceDeflects moving air
Frictional forceOpposes motion and reduces wind speed

Friction is particularly important near the Earth's surface, where vegetation, buildings and irregular terrain resist the movement of air. Its influence on wind speed and direction helps explain differences between atmospheric circulation over land and over oceans.

Wind direction and naming

Winds are conventionally named according to the direction from which they originate, not the direction towards which they travel.

  • An easterly wind comes from the east and travels generally westward.
  • A westerly wind comes from the west and travels generally eastward.
  • A northeasterly wind comes from the northeast and travels towards the southwest.
  • A southwesterly wind comes from the southwest and travels towards the northeast.

A wind moving from the Northern Hemisphere towards the Equator is initially moving southward. Its rightward Coriolis deflection gives it a westward component, producing the northeasterly direction characteristic of the Northern Hemisphere trade winds.

Prelims focus

  • Earth's rotation is from west to east.
  • Northern Hemisphere: rightward deflection.
  • Southern Hemisphere: leftward deflection.
  • Horizontal Coriolis effect is zero at the Equator and maximum at the poles for equal wind speeds.
  • At a given latitude, greater wind speed produces a greater Coriolis force.
  • Trap: A wind blowing towards the east is a westerly, not an easterly.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 3: Motions of the Earth, pp. 18–22; NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, 2025–26 reprint, Chapter 9, pp. 78–79; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 10: Winds, p. 70; NOAA National Ocean Service, The Coriolis Effect. Online sources consulted on 28 November 2026.]
